# 2 Maccabees Chapter 8 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 8 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_008_page_001.jpg

---

## Preamble

Chapter 8 marks the narrative turn from suffering to resistance. Judas Maccabeus organizes his forces, prays, and defeats Nicanor against overwhelming odds. The chapter follows the theological pattern established in chapters 5–7: the suffering of the faithful has satisfied God's disciplinary anger, and now God's mercy is operative. Three theological emphases shape the chapter: the prayer before battle (vv. 2–4), Judas's speech contrasting human arms with divine power (vv. 16–18), and the distribution of spoils to the vulnerable after victory (vv. 28, 30). The three agents agree on structure; PNEUMA dramatizes Judas's speech; EMET and LOGOS show close agreement throughout.

---

**1** Judas Maccabeus and his companions went about secretly into the villages, summoning their kinsfolk and enlisting those who had remained faithful to Judaism, until they had assembled about six thousand men.

**2** They called upon the LORD to look upon the people who were being oppressed on every side, to have compassion on the temple that had been profaned by godless men,

**3** to take pity on the city that was being destroyed and on the verge of being leveled to the ground, and to hearken to the blood that cried out to him,

**4** and to remember the lawless destruction of the innocent children and the blasphemies against his name, and to show his hatred of evil.

**5** As soon as Maccabeus had organized his forces, the Gentiles found him irresistible, for the LORD's anger had turned to mercy.

**6** Coming upon towns and villages by surprise, he burned them and retook the most favorable positions, putting to flight a considerable number of the enemy.

**7** He found night attacks especially suitable for such operations. His valor was talked about everywhere.

**8** When Philip saw that the man was gaining ground little by little, and that his advances were becoming more frequent and more successful, he wrote to Ptolemy, the governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, requesting reinforcement.

**9** Ptolemy promptly appointed Nicanor son of Patroclus, one of the king's First Friends, and dispatched him in command of no fewer than twenty thousand armed men drawn from various nations, to wipe out the entire race of Judea. He also assigned Gorgias to serve with him — a general with experience in military affairs.

**10** Nicanor resolved to raise for the king the tribute owed to the Romans, amounting to two thousand talents, by selling the captured Jews as slaves.

**11** He immediately sent word to the coastal cities, inviting them to buy Jewish slaves and promising to hand over ninety at a talent — little anticipating the judgment that was about to overtake him from the Almighty.

**12** When word reached Judas of Nicanor's invasion, he informed his companions of the arrival of the army.

**13** Those who were cowardly and had lost faith in God's justice deserted and made off.

**14** The rest sold all their remaining possessions and together besought the LORD to rescue those whom the ungodly Nicanor had already sold as slaves before the battle even began —

**15** if not for their own sake, then at least for the sake of the covenants made with their ancestors, and because he had called them by his holy and glorious name.

**16** Maccabeus assembled his men — six thousand in number — and exhorted them not to be panic-stricken at the enemy nor frightened by the great multitude of Gentiles who were attacking them without just cause, but to fight with all their courage,

**17** keeping before their eyes the lawless outrage perpetrated against the holy place, the cruel mockery inflicted on the city, and the destruction of their ancestral way of life.

**18** "For they trust in weapons and in feats of daring," he said. "But we trust in the almighty God, who with a single nod is able to strike down those who are coming against us and even the whole world."

**19** He also recounted the occasions when help came to their ancestors: how in the time of Sennacherib a hundred and eighty-five thousand had been destroyed,

**20** and how in the battle with the Galatians in Babylonia, eight thousand Jews together with four thousand Macedonians — when the Macedonians were hard pressed — destroyed one hundred and twenty thousand through the help that came from heaven, and received great spoil.

**21** With these words he filled them with great courage and made them ready to die for their laws and their fatherland. Then he divided his force into four parts.

**22** He appointed his brothers Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan each to command a division, placing fifteen hundred men under each.

**23** He also appointed Eleazar to read aloud from the holy scriptures, and gave the watchword "God's help." Leading the first division himself, he joined battle with Nicanor.

**24** With the Almighty as their ally, they killed more than nine thousand of the enemy, wounded and disabled the greater part of Nicanor's forces, and compelled all of them to flee.

**25** They also seized the money of those who had come to buy them as slaves. After pursuing the enemy for some distance, they were obliged to break off because the hour was late.

**26** For it was the day before the sabbath, and for that reason they did not prolong the pursuit.

**27** When they had collected the arms of the enemy and stripped them of their spoils, they kept the sabbath, offering abundant praise and thanks to the LORD who had saved them on that day and had begun to show them his mercy.

**28** After the sabbath, they distributed part of the spoils to those who had been tortured, to the widows, and to the orphans; the remainder they divided among themselves and their children.

**29** When they had done this, they made common supplication and implored the merciful LORD to be fully reconciled with his servants.

**30** In engagements with the forces of Timothy and Bacchides they killed more than twenty thousand of them, gained possession of some very high strongholds, and divided a large amount of plunder — giving equal shares to those who had been tortured, to the orphans, the widows, and the elderly.

**31** They collected the arms of the enemy and stored them all carefully in strategic places, and carried the rest of the spoils to Jerusalem.

**32** They killed the commander of Timothy's forces, a most wicked man who had greatly harmed the Jews.

**33** While they were celebrating the victory in the city of their ancestors, they burned Callisthenes and some others — men who had set fire to the sacred gates and who had fled into one small house. These received fitting recompense for their impiety.

**34** The three-times-accursed Nicanor, who had brought the thousand merchants to buy the Jews,

**35** was brought low with the help of the LORD by the very people he had expected to sell as slaves. He stripped off his splendid uniform, made his way alone through the interior like a fugitive slave, and reached Antioch — having achieved nothing except the destruction of his own army.

**36** Thus the man who had undertaken to secure tribute for the Romans by selling the people of Jerusalem declared publicly that the Jews had a defender, and that they were invulnerable because they followed the laws he had ordained.

---

## Translator's Notes

- **v. 1, "remained faithful to Judaism"**: Greek *emmenontas tē Ioudaismos* — those who had remained in Judaism. This is one of the earliest uses of "Judaism" (*Ioudaismos*) as a term for the Jewish religious way of life, as distinct from Hellenism.
- **v. 9, "First Friends"**: The highest court rank in the Seleucid system, above regular "Friends." The designation of Nicanor as a First Friend underscores the magnitude of the force sent against Judas.
- **v. 11, "ninety for a talent"**: A talent was approximately 30 kilograms of silver. This price per slave tells us something about both the scale of the operation Nicanor envisioned and the casual contempt for Jewish life it represents.
- **v. 20, the Galatian battle**: This battle in Babylonia is not otherwise attested in our sources and may derive from Jason of Cyrene's lost history. The point is illustrative: a small Jewish force had previously defeated overwhelming odds with divine aid.
- **vv. 22–23, the battle order**: The division into four parts, with Judas leading one himself and reading from the scriptures before battle, has deep resonances with the traditions of holy war (cf. Deuteronomy 20, 1 Maccabees).
- **v. 26, "day before the sabbath"**: The fighters' halt at the eve of the sabbath, even in hot pursuit, is theologically significant. This is presented as piety, not weakness — in contrast to those in chapter 6 who refused to fight on the sabbath and died for it. The distinction is: defensive fighting on the sabbath is permitted; unnecessary continuation of offensive fighting is not.
- **vv. 28, 30, distribution of spoils**: The deliberate sharing of spoils with the tortured, widows, orphans, and elderly is a theological statement about the purpose of victory. Judas's war is not for personal enrichment but for the restoration of the community.
